title: Microburst routing insurance scenarios
content:
Purpose / context:
This is a working note exploring the idea of a lightweight 'insurance' layer for microburst traffic: short-duration spikes (0.5–10s) that are high QPS but low aggregate token volume. Goal is to outline cost models and routing knobs that trade a small predictable spend for significantly lower user-facing latency failure rates during microbursts.

Definitions / baseline assumptions:
- Microburst: sudden increase in request rate for a single customer or route lasting between 0.5s–10s, with median per-request tokens = 40.
- Hot-window SLO: 95th percentile tail latency under 200ms for interactive chat routes.
- Cost units: $/GPU-hour and $/1k tokens (hosted). For rough math we use: on-demand GPU = $3.50/hr, spot GPU = $0.85/hr, dedicated (reserved) amortized = $1.80/hr. Average throughput per GPU (small seq workloads): 200 tokens/sec conservative.
- Service behavior: requests that can’t be placed on GPU immediately are queued or routed to a cheaper fallback (smaller model) with latency impact.

Why 'insurance' model?
- Full overprovisioning to meet 99.99% microburst SLOs is expensive and underutilized most of the time.
- Spot capacity is cheap but volatile and often insufficient at <10s timescales because preemption and provisioning delays can matter.
- On-demand capacity is reliable but expensive if kept idle.
- Insurance = small pool (elastic) of rapidly provisionable on-demand capacity or prewarmed containers that we hold for short durations or quickly acquire on spike detection, plus policy to fall back to a lower-cost path when insurance is exhausted.

Scenarios to model (spreadsheet-friendly):
1) Reactive on-demand+prewarm: 2 on-demand instances prewarmed for N routes, warm start <1s. Insurance cost = hold cost + spin-up buffer.
2) Spot+on-demand hybrid: attempt spot first, if insufficient failover to on-demand insurance pool. Measure preemption risk.
3) Model ladder fallback: if primary model full, route to quantized model variant (Q4) with small latency uplift but lower throughput; or to 1.5x smaller architecture (faster, cheaper) for microbursts.
4) Queue + degrade: accept queuing for up to Tq milliseconds then degrade to fallback model if queue exceeds threshold.

Key variables for spreadsheet columns:
- route_id, baseline_qps, burst_peak_qps, burst_duration_s, avg_tokens_per_req, pct_requests_user_retries, cost_primary_per_token, cost_fallback_per_token, on_demand_hold_hours_per_day, spot_success_rate, prewarm_instances, spinup_time_s, SLA_penalty_cost_per_violation.

Simple cost math (examples):
- Token processing capacity per GPU in burst window: tokens_per_gpu = throughput_tokens_sec * burst_duration_s. For burst duration 5s and throughput 200 tok/s => 1000 tokens per GPU.
- On-demand hour-equivalent of a microburst: if you reserve 1 on-demand GPU for 2 minutes/day on average, daily cost = 2/60 * 3.5 = $0.1167/day (~$42.6/yr).
- Compare to cost of degraded responses: if degraded model increases avg latency and causes 0.5% revenue loss or $0.02/user impact per hit, and you expect 10M requests/year for this route, expected annual cost = 0.005 * 10M * 0.02 = $1,000. Insurance could be cheaper.

Microburst example table (paste into sheet):
route_id,baseline_qps,burst_peak_qps,burst_duration_s,avg_tokens,primary_cost_per_token, fallback_cost_per_token,prewarm_instances,spinup_time_s,spot_success_rate
chat-ux-A,2,25,6,40,0.000004,0.0000025,2,0.8,0.6
search-emb-B,10,120,3,16,0.000003,0.0000015,1,0.6,0.7

Compute per-burst cost (chat-ux-A):
- Primary tokens at peak: 25 req/s * 6s * 40 tok = 6000 tokens per burst.
- If primary can only service baseline capacity (2 req/s), deficit = 23 req/s * 6s * 40 = 5520 tokens must be handled by insurance/fallback.
- If fallback (quantized) handles tokens at fallback_cost_per_token=0.0000025 => burst fallback cost = 5520 * 0.0000025 = $0.0138 per burst.
- If we prewarm 2 on-demand GPUs to absorb the delta for full 6s: capacity per GPU = 200 tok/s * 6s = 1200 tokens => 2 GPUs = 2400 tokens (not enough), need 5 GPUs -> cost to hold them for 6s: 5 GPUs * (6/3600)hr * $3.5/hr = $0.0292 per burst.
- Observations: fallback model is cheaper per-burst for small bursts; prewarmed on-demand becomes competitive when SLA penalties are high or fallback quality loss is unacceptable.

Risk modeling for Spot fallback (Monte Carlo notes):
- Model spot success as Bernoulli with p = spot_success_rate. For each simulated microburst event draw k spot instances; if any fail, fallback to on-demand insurance or fallback model.
- Compute expected cost = p * (spot provisioning cost + spin-up effect) + (1-p) * (fallback_cost + SLA_penalty).
- Important to include preemption tail: if spot instance preempts mid-burst, request reroutes cause extra latency; treat as partial SLA violation proportional to fraction of burst served.

Insurance policy knobs (implementation notes):
- route-level SLA tiering: premium routes get on-demand prewarm pool (configurable hours/day), standard routes get spot-first with small on-demand standby, free routes get model-degrade-first.
- microburst detection: rolling 200ms window; trigger if > X * baseline_qps AND absolute spike > Y requests. Tuning: X=6, Y=10 as starting point.
- Hold vs on-demand spinup tradeoff: maintaining N prewarm instances reduces spinup_time but costs hold_hours. Consider schedule-based hold windows (e.g., business hours) and predictive holds triggered by anomaly models.
- Fallback hierarchy (policy): 1) local cache/KV prefix reuse 2) quantized faster variant 3) smaller architecture 4) on-demand insurance pool 5) queue with timeout -> error. Order can be changed per route.

Experiment plan (short):
- Phase 0 (simulation): run event-driven sim over 30 days of traffic (use historical traffic traces) to compute burst distribution and candidate insurance sizes. Outputs: expected annual cost, expected SLA violations avoided, p90 cost per burst.
- Phase 1 (canary): enable for 5 low-risk routes with prewarm_instances=1 for 2 weeks. Monitor: tail latency, requests routed to fallback, cost delta.
- Phase 2: ramp and add predictive prewarm windows for top 20 routes.

Metrics to track in console dashboards:
- microburst_count_by_route, avg_burst_peak_qps, avg_burst_duration_s, pct_bursts_served_by_insurance, pct_bursts_routed_to_fallback, incremental_cost_insurance, SLA_violation_rate_during_bursts.
- Add a synthetic metric: insurance_ROI = (SLA_penalty_costs_avoided / insurance_costs) aggregated monthly.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to attribute cost to customers vs product (should we charge insurance as a premium feature)?
- Best default for prewarm_instances per route: static 1 or dynamic based on 30d P99 burst size?
- Implementation gap: fast spinup under 1s possible for containers or do we need cold start mitigations at infra layer? See infra ticket JIRA-INF-842.
- UX: expose a slider in Console for "microburst insurance level" (off / small / medium / large) with estimated monthly cost.

Quick heuristics (for docs and decision-making):
- If expected annual cost of customer-visible degradation > 5x insurance hold cost => default to insurance.
- For bursts < 10s and delta tokens per burst < 10k, prefer fallback quantized model by default.
- If route is revenue-critical or enterprise with SLA, prefer standby on-demand pool.

Notes to self / short checklist before drafting PR:
- Export simulation notebook to optimize/simulations/microburst-insurance.ipynb (pull traffic traces).
- Add a small telemetry tag to routed requests so we can measure fallback quality delta. Todo: PR in routing repo.
- Draft Console copy for slider and cost estimate: product copy to coordinate with UX.

References and related work:
- internal: CONFLUENCE-OPT-77 (routing insurance design doc)
- infra: JIRA-INF-842 (spinup perf investigations)
- prior experiments: routing/pull/411 (spot fallback implementation prototype)

End of working note.

(Short, rough — intended as an input to the team spreadsheet + sim notebook. Comments welcome.)
